findings.title: Application-specific repository policy conflicts with the shared repository ledger
findings.minimal_counterexample: Commission one repository R serving valid apps A and B under the same publisher and metadata root. Install A, leaving a ready generation with policy hash PA. DiscoveryPolicy embeds appId and requires every entry to have that app, so B necessarily has different discovery bytes and a different RepositoryPolicy hash PB. Start B's first installation. It must open R's existing ledger, but that ledger has one current policy hash PA, while B's signed Host pins PB. Policy changes require an authenticated planned transition from an admitted installed source; fresh B has no such source. Refusing blocks an otherwise supported fresh installation; overwriting PA changes A's repository policy; using a new ledger loses the stipulated shared repository history.
findings.invariant: A repository's root/role/time floors are shared and stable across apps, while app-scoped signed policy remains independently bound. A new app cannot need another app's installed-update-key transition merely to use the repository.
findings.smallest_correction: Separate repository-wide trust/transport policy from app-specific discovery/publisher bindings, or define an authenticated multi-policy per-app binding table beneath the same floor ledger. Specify how a fresh app is admitted and how a transition affects only its own binding without resetting shared floors. Do not solve this by namespacing floors with the policy digest.
evidence: identity.md:201-202 puts publisherPolicySha256 and discoveryPolicySha256 in RepositoryPolicy; identity.md:214-221 makes DiscoveryPolicy app-specific.
windows.md:179 explicitly shares one repository namespace across apps; metadata.md:181 stores one policySha256 and metadata.md:295 binds admission to the current policy digest.
metadata.md:164 requires the identity owner's authenticated transition for a changed policy; identity.md:251-272 derives that transition from an admitted source artifact.

findings.title: Committed provenance cannot address the policy evidence it is required to retain
findings.minimal_counterexample: Complete a fresh v2 installation with recovery_bindings empty, then restart without the acquisition bundle. Recovery and ordinary verification need the exact installed repository, issuer, discovery and recovery policy bytes. The closed v3 record contains policy hash scalars, but no evidence reference, attempt ID, or evidence-set locator. D-9 stores the immutable bytes at evidence/transitions/<attemptId>/<kind>/<sha256>; its reference object also omits attemptId. A fresh installation has no transition journal from which to obtain that missing component. The initial-admission record names an attempt but is itself indexed by that unknown attempt and is not referenced by provenance. The draft supplies no bounded authenticated lookup/index or fresh policy-set publication/retention rule.
findings.invariant: A committed protected installation must independently locate and verify every retained authority object after restart, without arbitrary path input, unbounded search, or reconstruction from feed/caller bytes.
findings.smallest_correction: Use a derivable global content-addressed policy location, or add one exact bounded evidence-set locator/reference to v3 provenance and include it in the lifecycle hash. Define the initial installer as the publisher of that set before final provenance, its readback gate, and its retention independently of pending/retained transition sets. Keep digest, length, type, protection, and decoder checks.
evidence: identity.md:291 enumerates all v3 top-level fields; 303-305 closes browser bindings. Fresh provenance has no attempt/evidence locator and recovery_bindings may be empty (312).

identity.md:336-340 defines references only as kind,sha256,bytes but paths require an additional attemptId; 353-354 requires authenticated policy references and prohibits reconstruction of missing objects.
recovery.md:104-108 requires installed provenance to retain authenticated repository/recovery policy references using D-9; the exact v3 grammar does not supply those references.
recovery.md:214-240 gives initial admissions an attempt-scoped filename but does not put that attempt into provenance or freeze initial policy-evidence publication.
findings.first_acceptance_check: After a fresh v2 commit, discard all acquisition inputs and in-memory state, leave no transition journal, restart, and resolve every required policy from the closed provenance plus authenticated repository root using only specified bounded path rules. Exercise missing/wrongly protected objects as refusal controls.

findings.title: The repository-global policy slot cannot support the stated cross-app namespace
findings.owning_invariant: One stable repository ledger across apps must preserve trust floors, while every policy change requires the identity owner's authenticated successor.
minimal_counterexample: Commission one RepositoryId R for fresh apps A and B, as windows.md:179 permits.
A's RepositoryPolicy pins a DiscoveryPolicy with appId A; B's pins one with appId B. The policies necessarily have different digests.
Installing A leaves the single generation.policySha256 equal to A's digest.
B opens the same R ledger. Accepting its different policy requires the D-7 transition, but a fresh B has no admitted current B artifact or installed B U1 signature.
findings.impact: The implementation must either reject the advertised second-app fresh-install cell or silently replace repository policy without the required transition. The same global slot also prevents both app policies from remaining current together.
findings.smallest_correction: Explicitly scope each commissioned RepositoryId to one app and remove the cross-app claim, or separate repository-global metadata policy from bounded per-app acquisition/discovery policy. Preserve the shared metadata floors and bind the selected lane policy in admission evidence.
findings.first_falsifiable_check: One repository, two valid Host/candidate bundles for distinct appIds, no prior B installation: install A, then admit B, then refresh A. Both must work without lowering floors or inventing a source-U1 transition.

evidence.fact: Requires one repository namespace across apps.
RepositoryPolicy pins one DiscoveryPolicy, which names one app and requires every entry to use that app.
One current generation has one policy digest; changed policy requires the identity successor and ReadyRevision binds the current policy digest.
A planned transition requires an admitted current source artifact and installed-U1 signature.

findings.title: Add a client correction for threshold-only root changes preserving old-role floors
findings.owning_invariant: D-24 permits counter reset on role-key-set change only; unchanged key sets preserve trusted timestamp, snapshot, and targets version floors.
minimal_counterexample: The protected store contains timestamp v100 signed by K1 under a root whose timestamp keys are {K1,K2} with threshold 1.
A valid successor root changes the threshold to 2 without changing the keys. D-24 intentionally does not reset the stored role.
Supply an unexpired timestamp v1 with valid signatures from K1 and K2.
Pinned tough's load_timestamp re-verifies old v100 under the new threshold; that fails and its conditional skips the v100 rollback comparison.
The analogous snapshot path can also skip snapshot and targets floors after a snapshot-threshold increase.
findings.impact: A client patched only for the listed D-20 differences can still accept a replayed lower-version graph after a threshold-only root update. Enforcing new-root signatures on the old cache instead would make legitimate threshold increases unrecoverable rather than preserving the old accepted floors.
findings.smallest_correction: Extend D-20 to require the client to compare every intact previously accepted role/floor independently of whether its old signature envelope satisfies the current root threshold, unless D-24 durably authorized a key-set reset. Define the trusted-store handoff and add a threshold-only regression for both timestamp and snapshot.
findings.first_falsifiable_check: With unchanged keys and threshold 1->2, old singly signed v100 must remain the floor; a valid doubly signed v1 must fail and v101 must pass. The isolated mutant restoring the current-root-authentication guard must accept the lower replay and turn RED.

All timestamp/snapshot-description rollback comparisons are inside root.signed.verify_role(&old_timestamp).is_ok().
Snapshot and targets rollback comparisons similarly depend on current-root verification of the old snapshot.

findings.title: Define the shared-ancestor creation boundary before asserting zero installation-parent effects
findings.counterexample: Use a supported fresh standard-user account whose LocalAppData exists but GYLDLAB does not. The repository store and durable admission record must be created beneath LocalAppData/GYLDLAB/Keld/acquisition-v1 before the permit can authorize installation creation. This necessarily first creates GYLDLAB and Keld, which are also missing parents of the v2 installation root. AC-44 and D-46 currently forbid creation of any installation parent before admission. Treating those components as acquisition work makes the implementation feasible, but that narrowing is never stated in the effect rule or census oracle.
findings.invariant: Every filesystem effect has one explicit authority and classification; the fresh-user path must be able to establish acquisition state without silently violating the promised no-installation-parent-before-admission boundary.
findings.impact: The draft has two plausible incompatible implementations: refusing a genuinely fresh user because acquisition cannot create the common parents, or creating them while still claiming the blanket no-parent-effect result on a later admission refusal. This is a design-scope ambiguity, not proof of a native exploit.
findings.smallest_correction: Explicitly assign the shared GYLDLAB/Keld ancestors to bounded acquisition-namespace preparation after offline managed-owner preflight and actual-worker admission. Define the installation-specific first-effect boundary (including v2/leaf scaffolding) separately, and update AC-44/D-46 and the refusal effect statements to use that boundary. Alternatively place acquisition below an independently provisioned namespace. Add a clean-user census case that begins above GYLDLAB and verifies each authority boundary.

windows.md:259-260 and recovery.md:214-237 require the external admission record before any missing installation parent is created.
Pinned native windows_fs.rs:452-488 uses a retained parent RootDirectory and one validated child component; parents must already exist for relative descendant creation.
A read-only PureWindowsPath comparison confirmed GYLDLAB/Keld is the shared prefix; this was a textual topology check, not a Windows run.

independent_refutation.reasoning: A consistent implementation can classify GYLDLAB/Keld as acquisition work under D-44, but identity/integration do not supply the missing explicit exemption and AC-44 still says no installation parent. Do not describe the whole design as intrinsically impossible.

MR-02.bounded_conclusion: The exact pinned upstream client skips stored timestamp and snapshot rollback floors when an increased current threshold makes a previously accepted old envelope fail re-verification. R2 preserves those records for unchanged key sets but does not require a correction to this conditional. This is a specification correction gap, not an executed product exploit or an assertion that an unimplemented adapter already behaves incorrectly.
minimal_counterexample: Root R1 assigns timestamp and snapshot keys K1,K2 with threshold 1. The protected store contains accepted timestamp v100 and snapshot v100, each carrying one valid K1 signature.
A properly root-authorized R2 keeps exactly K1,K2 but raises both thresholds to 2. The root version increment, root signature thresholds, expiry, transport and digest checks all pass.
R2 metadata.md:219-230 gives unchanged key fingerprints because threshold is explicitly excluded. Consequently it retains the v100 role references and their rollback floors.

A replay supplies still-unexpired timestamp v1 and matching snapshot v1, each historically signed by both K1 and K2, with matching hashes and lengths. No new private-key access is needed for this replay assumption.

The incoming roles pass R2 threshold 2. The stored one-signature v100 envelopes fail R2 threshold 2. At upstream lib.rs:934 and :1096, this failure skips the entire old-version and downstream-version comparison blocks. The historical v100 floors do not participate in admission.

direct_evidence.fact: Authenticates the new timestamp under the current root, but compares trusted timestamp and snapshot versions only inside root.signed.verify_role(&old_timestamp).is_ok(), then stores the accepted incoming timestamp.
Authenticates the incoming snapshot, but old snapshot and targets-floor comparisons are conditional on current-root verification of the stored old snapshot.
verify_role selects role keys from self (the current Root) and requires valid signatures >= role_keys.threshold. A stored one-signature envelope fails after a threshold-only change to 2.
The reset fingerprint covers key IDs and canonical public-key bytes, excludes role threshold, and clears downstream references only if one of those key-set fingerprints changes.

The correction table does not cover the current-threshold guard on historical rollback comparisons. Protected readback guarantees bytes, bounds, digests, parse results and role identity. Preserving references and the equal-version fix do not themselves remove the guard for a lower incoming version.
The specified reset condition is timestamp/snapshot key rotation; retained trusted timestamp versions must prevent rollback. A threshold-only change is not stated as a key-rotation reset.

attempted_refutations: Key rotation reset: fails to refute because key IDs and key bytes are unchanged; R2 explicitly omits the threshold.

Protected store validation: fails to refute because all retained bytes are well-formed, authentic when accepted, correctly hashed, and protected. Their failure under a stronger later threshold is not corruption.
Equal-version correction: fails to refute because v1 is lower than v100, not equal.
Expiry or coherent-graph validation: fails to refute when the historical two-signature v1 graph remains unexpired and its lengths/hashes agree.

Generic floor-preservation prose: states the desired invariant but does not identify or change the incompatible pinned-client branch. An adapter that instead insists on re-verifying historical cache under the new threshold may refuse safely, but its legitimate threshold-increase liveness and accepted-floor handoff still need an explicit contract.
MR-02.smallest_correction: Add a pinned-client correction and acceptance case: unless an authorized key-set reset occurred, compare every incoming role and downstream version against protected historically accepted floors independently of whether the stored old signature envelope satisfies the newest threshold. Continue to authenticate incoming metadata under the current root. Do not add thresholds to the reset fingerprint as a shortcut.
MR-02.first_acceptance_check: Use unchanged K1,K2 with threshold 1->2, retained one-signature v100, replayed two-signature unexpired v1, and legitimate two-signature v101. v1 must refuse, v101 must proceed, and both results must hold after a restart between root publication and role refresh.
MR-02.execution_limit: Source and specification reasoning only. No Rust client execution, product adapter, native Windows, or production signatures were run.
